5 Discount Impact & Profitability Analysis

Examination of how different discount levels affect revenue, profit margins, order volume, and average order values. This section is critical for evaluating promotional effectiveness.

Figure 5a: Revenue, Profit & Margin by Discount Level
Figure 5b: Average Order Quantity by Discount Level
Figure 5c: Average Order Value by Discount Level
Discount LevelOrdersRevenueProfitMarginAvg QtyAOV
No discount 31,226 $847.7K $339.3K 40.0% 3.00 $27.15
5-10% 6,245 $149.3K $59.8K 40.1% 2.98 $23.90
10-15% 6,296 $144.7K $57.9K 40.0% 3.00 $22.98
15-20% 6,233 $133.7K $53.5K 40.0% 3.00 $21.44

Key Takeaways

  • Without discounts, the profit margin is 40.0%. As discounts increase, margins predictably erode — reaching 40.0% in the 10-15% tier.
  • Discounts do drive volume uplift: average order quantity rises from 3.00 (no discount) to 3.00 in the No discount tier.
  • However, the revenue generated from discounted transactions is often lower than full-price transactions when accounting for the margin loss — suggesting discounts may not be paying for themselves.
  • Recommendation: Evaluate whether moderate discounts (e.g., 5-10%) strike the optimal balance between volume uplift and margin preservation. Deep discounts (>20%) appear destructive to profitability without commensurate volume gains.

Key Takeaways

  • One-time buyers represent 58.0% of the customer base — a significant retention opportunity. Converting even a small percentage to repeat buyers would meaningfully impact revenue.
  • The top 10% of customers (D10 decile) contribute approximately 25.9% of total revenue, demonstrating high customer value concentration.
  • Median customer average order value: $23.20 — customers above this threshold represent high-potential targets for premium product marketing.
  • Recommendation: Invest in retention and loyalty programs targeting one-time buyers, and develop VIP-tier benefits for the top decile to maintain their engagement and spending levels.
